name: Ear candling

lead: Ear candling is a spa and alternative-health practice in which a hollow cone made of fabric and wax is lit at its wide end while the narrow end rests at the opening of the ear canal. Practitioners and sellers present it as a way to draw out earwax and impurities, so the ears look and feel clean, and as a relaxing grooming ritual.

The proposed mechanism is a gentle suction created by the burning candle. Measurements published in the clinical literature, including a 1996 study cited by encyclopedic sources, found no negative pressure, and the residue left in the candle stub resembles that of candles burned without an ear. Medical bodies and regulators have issued warnings about the practice.

paras: The person lies on their side while a second person holds the candle upright, with a card or foil disc to catch drips. The candle burns down for roughly 10 to 20 minutes and is then extinguished and sometimes cut open so the residue can be shown. It is usually offered in salons and holistic clinics, though home kits are sold.

Reported harms include burns to the ear, face and hair, candle wax blocking the canal, and perforated eardrums; fires have also been reported. The US FDA and Health Canada have issued public warnings, and Health Canada treats sales as illegal. Children are described as particularly at risk.

angle.text: Proponents use ear candling as a cleaning and relaxation ritual aimed at clearing wax from the outer ear. Measurements of candle pressure and residue have not found the suction effect that sellers describe.

lead: Ear candling, also called ear coning or thermal-auricular therapy, is an alternative-health practice in which a hollow cone of fabric soaked in wax is burned with its narrow end placed at the ear canal opening. Users and sellers describe it as a gentle way to remove earwax and impurities, relieve ear and sinus discomfort and leave a feeling of clean, relaxed ears.[1][2]

For appearance, the practice sits within ear and head grooming: proponents see clean, wax-free ears as part of a tidy, healthy look, and some sessions are offered as a relaxation treatment alongside facials or massage. The candle typically measures about 10 inches and burns for 10 to 20 minutes while the person lies on one side.[1][2]

Researchers who have tested the mechanism report that candles do not generate suction and do not remove wax.[2] Clinical guidelines on earwax management and a series of case reports have documented injuries, and agencies including the US FDA and Health Canada have issued warnings.[2][3][4] The practice is discussed here as a documented fringe grooming and wellness ritual.
infobox: Cotton or linen cone coated in paraffin or beeswax
FDA alert (2007); sale for health claims illegal in Canada
Hopi ear candles (name disputed by the Hopi Tribal Council)

paras: The candle is a tapered tube of cotton, linen or muslin soaked in paraffin, beeswax or soy wax, about 9 to 12 inches long. Some brands add herbs or essential oils.[1] The person lies on their side, the pointed end is held at the ear opening, and a protective plate or foil shields the face and hair from drips. The candle is lit at the top and burns down for 10 to 20 minutes.[1][2]
Afterward, the stub may be opened to show a dark residue, which sellers present as removed wax. Clinical writers report that candles burned without being placed in an ear leave comparable residue.[2]

Encyclopedic accounts trace the practice mainly to the United States in the 20th century, with later spread through alternative-health shops and the internet.[2] Promoters have attributed it to Egyptians, Greeks, Chinese or Native American peoples. The Hopi Tribal Council has stated that the practice is not and has never been Hopi, in response to candles sold under the Hopi name.[2]

Sellers claim the burning candle creates a chimney effect that draws wax, bacteria and toxins from the canal, and that sessions relieve sinus pressure, glue ear, tinnitus, migraines and stress.[1][5] Related claims describe energy balancing or spiritual cleansing.[1]

A 2022 Saudi survey of otolaryngology patients and others examined the use of ear candling during COVID-19 lockdowns, when clinic visits were restricted, showing that some people turned to it as a home alternative.[6]

A 1996 study by an ENT clinic in Spokane reported that candling produced no negative pressure and did not remove wax.[2] A 2007 Canadian Family Physician review concluded that it showed no reliable positive effect and recommended that general practitioners discourage it.[7] A 2016 systematic review of complementary options for otitis media listed ear candling among therapies whose scientific support had not been demonstrated.[8] A case report in the European Journal of General Practice summarized the literature as showing no evidence of effectiveness and possible ear damage.[5]

The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery guideline on earwax lists what clinicians do for impacted wax and advises against ear candling as a way to treat it.[3] A 2018 American Family Physician review also covers earwax management and the removal methods recommended by physicians.[9]

Case reports describe a 4-year-old with candle wax in the canal and hearing loss attributed to candling.[10][5] Reported complications in the literature include burns of the face, ear and hair, wax obstruction of the ear canal and perforated eardrums.[2][7] Encyclopedic accounts mention at least two house fires, one fatal, linked to candling accidents.[2]

The FDA issued an alert in 2007 describing ear candles as dangerous when used as labeled, and Health Canada considers sale illegal, even when marketed for entertainment.[2] Nursing and medical journals have printed warnings.[11][12]

Controlled work is limited: a 1996 study measured pressure in the canal during candling and found no suction, and residue analysis found no difference from candles burned freely.[2] A 2007 review of the literature found no reliable benefit,[7] and a 2016 systematic review on otitis media noted that the therapy lacked demonstrated efficacy.[8] The AAO-HNSF earwax guideline states that candling is not recommended for impaction.[3]
